item.title: When Polynomial Multiplication Counts Geometry: Schubert Polynomials and Monk's Rule
item.description: arXiv:2610.35944v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a geometric introduction to Schubert polynomial multiplication through point-line flags in the complex projective plane. Moving a prescribed point onto a prescribed line gives a family with local equation $au=\lambda$, whose limiting curve has two components. The incidence equations and their local multiplicities give a two-term divisor product, using the standard intersection product on classes of algebraic cycles. Permutation labels and Schubert polynomials express the same decomposition as an instance of Monk's rule. For three incidence conditions, each allowing either a point on a prescribed line or a line through a prescribed point, the product has degree six. Under explicit general-position assumptions, direct construction and local equations give six distinct solutions of multiplicity one.
item.dc:creator: Ryan Bansal

item.title: On the frieze patterns by Conway and Coxeter
item.description: arXiv:2610.35968v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The story of frieze patterns started in 1970s with a paper by Coxeter and two short papers by Conway and Coxeter, one listing questions and the other providing brief answers. During the first three decades it was followed by only a handful of papers observing some further properties of the same objects. Then Propp (2005) and Caldero and Chapoton (2006) established connections between frieze patterns and the recent theory of cluster algebras introduced by Fomin and Zelevinsky in early 2000s. Since then the theory of frieze patterns exploded with new results, and frieze patterns found a wide spectrum of connections in various domains of mathematics, including combinatorics, geometry, representation theory and integrable systems. The literature on frieze patterns grew vastly and continues to expand. In this note we give a brief overview of some of the directions emerging from the papers by Conway and Coxeter and single out core ideas which were later replayed in different contexts.
item.dc:creator: Anna Felikson, Pavel Tumarkin

item.title: Quadratic Reciprocity via Vandermonde Matrix
item.description: arXiv:2610.35990v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents a proof of the law of quadratic reciprocity using the Vandermonde matrix and Zolotarev's lemma.
item.dc:creator: Hongshen Chua

item.title: Building Mathematical Software -- Lessons from the Development of GAP
item.description: arXiv:2610.36300v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mathematical software has particular needs that are not all covered by the existing literature on software engineering or algorithm design. This paper looks at some of these aspects, in the concrete context of the computer algebra system GAP. It also studies the potential impact AI systems could have on the development process for mathematical software.
item.dc:creator: Alexander Hulpke

item.title: Mathematical Reality Capture: from the age of discoveries to mathematical topography and surveys
item.description: arXiv:2610.37260v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A proof answers a precise question, but mathematical understanding also grows through the relationships that its answer makes visible. A point measurement likewise differs from a photograph or a three-dimensional reconstruction of a building. In this work, we argue that, with the help of AI, mathematics should move from a discipline focused on isolated investigations of mathematical objects towards one capable of mapping them systematically. We therefore introduce the idea of "Mathematical Reality Capture", inspired by digital surveying and the reconstruction of a scene from several viewpoints. An elementary example shows how comparing algebra and geometry can illuminate the same phenomenon, provided that we distinguish diversity of explanations from validity of proof. From this analogy we derive criteria for building verifiable atlases, an experiment with which to assess their usefulness, and a reflection on the role of mathematicians in interpreting them.
item.dc:creator: Daniele Corradetti

item.title: Notes on a strongly aperiodic monotile in $E^3$
item.description: arXiv:2609.24779v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We provide a clearer presentation of the Chair44 monotile, a new strongly aperiodic monotile in three-dimensional Euclidean space $E^3$.
item.dc:creator: Chaim Goodman-Strauss

item.title: A Central Limit Theorem for High-Temperature SYK Model: A case study on mathematical research using AI and Lean
item.description: arXiv:2610.18440v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Sachdev--Ye--Kitaev (SYK) model is a quantum many-body model of Majorana fermions with all-to-all random interactions. It has attracted wide interest in condensed matter and high-energy physics as a solvable model of non-Fermi liquids and holography. Fix an even integer $q\geq4$, and let $Z_N(\beta)$ be the partition function of the Gaussian $q$-body SYK model. We prove that for all sufficiently small inverse temperatures $\beta > 0$, there exists $\rho=\rho(\beta)>0$ such that \[ N^{q/2 -1}(\log Z_N(\beta)-\mathbb{E}[\log Z_N(\beta)]) \Longrightarrow \mathcal{N}(0,\rho^2). \] In addition to the mathematical results, we discuss how the proofs were developed and refined through interaction between human researchers and AI, and we describe the subsequent formalization of the main arguments in Lean 4. This work thus serves as a case study of a research workflow that integrates human insight, AI-assisted exploration, iterative proof refinement, and formal verification.
item.dc:creator: Yoshinori Kamijima, Shuta Nakajima, Ryoichiro Noda, K\^{o}hei Sasaya
